canonical_topic: Marginal bid clustering under uniform clearing price
definition: Because every cleared generator in a power auction is paid the same clearing price regardless of its own bid, a plant loses nothing by bidding just below a higher-cost competitor as long as that competitor (or someone else) ends up setting a higher price.
core_idea: The single-clearing-price mechanism removes any penalty for underbidding a rival, so similarly-positioned generators cluster their bids near common price points, and only the handful of plants actually on the margin end up setting the market price.
key_points: Uniform pricing means a generator doesn't need to be the top bidder to capture the clearing price, so there's no cost to bidding just under a higher-cost competitor.
This incentive causes generators with similar production costs to cluster their bids around the same price levels.
At any given time only a small number of plants are actually on the margin, so those few plants have outsized influence on the clearing price.
Because clustering behavior is predictable, it is often possible to infer which type of plant is currently setting the price by observing the stack.
trading_implications: Watching which cost tier of plants clusters near the margin helps predict which unit type is setting price and how sensitive price is to small shifts in demand or outages.
caveats: Being the highest bidder does not mean earning more revenue — since everyone clears at the same price, rational bidders intentionally underbid the next higher-cost unit rather than bidding at their true willingness-to-accept.
